text:
Carrot.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Fresh carrots have a sweet, earthy flavour rarely matched by shop-bought roots. Establishment can be tricky: germination is slow and slugs attack seedlings. Deep, fine, stone-free soil helps roots grow straight and tender; light soil or compost-filled no-dig beds can work well. Sow short successions for early-summer to autumn harvests. Steady moisture, careful thinning and carrot-fly protection make a big difference. Fresh manure, compaction, stones, drought and rough handling can leave roots forked, tough or damaged.

Apr – Jun

Harvest

Aug – Oct

Germination

17 days

Depth

1/2 in.

6 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

early: 8 lb; maincrop: 10 lb

Plant spacing

Thin to 2-3 in. apart

Ready in

Early ~12; maincrop ~16 weeks from sowing

Recommended varieties
SHORT-ROOTED
Early Nantes 2

A familiar early carrot with cylindrical roots. A practical general-purpose choice for successive sowings and tender young carrots.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Autumn King

A maincrop carrot producing substantial roots for autumn lifting and storage. Suits gardeners wanting a later, heavier crop.

INTERMEDIATE-ROOTED
Chantenay Red Cored

A shorter, broad-shouldered carrot. A useful alternative where very long-rooted varieties are less convenient to grow.

Key risks
Carrot fly

Tell-tale signs on carrots are reddish leaves which wilt in sunny weather and later turn yellow.

Fanging

Stones, compaction, fresh manure or unfinished compost can fork roots. Properly used mature compost is suitable for no-dig carrots.

Small roots

Aphids and virus will stunt growth and reduce yield, but even in the absence of pests and diseases many gardeners produce disappointingly small carrots.

Splitting

Much more serious than fanging of carrots, because the roots will not store.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
36
ROOT CROPS

Prepare the soil well.

Deep, fertile, stone-free and sandy soil is ideal.

Avoid fresh manure.

Follow a crop manured the previous year.

Weed young seedlings.

Weeds can easily smother them.

Soil & preparation
Use deep, fertile, sandy, stone-free soil; choose short-rooted varieties on heavy or stony ground. Improve clay well before sowing.
Follow a previously manured crop. Avoid fresh manure, which encourages forking; lime acid soil in winter and prepare a fine seedbed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow thinly

Sow direct, very thinly, in shallow drills.

2 Cover lightly

Cover lightly with fine soil or compost.

3 Thin later

Thin seedlings to the final spacing in Quick facts.

Mix seed with sand, sow into warmed soil and keep the seedbed moist. For November–December roots, sow a short-rooted variety in August; cover with cloches from October.

Looking after the crop
Thin only as needed in evenings or damp weather; water dry soil first. Firm afterwards and clear thinnings: bruised roots attract carrot fly.
Weed seedlings carefully; avoid hoeing close to established roots or loosening their soil.
In dry spells, soak evenly to root depth; light sprinkling is ineffective. Heavy watering after drought can split roots.
Keep young beds bare against slugs; clear early weeds before later sowings.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small carrots from June; baby roots may take eight weeks. Ease with a fork to limit disturbance.
Lift storage crops around October, earlier if carrot fly appears or before hard frost and very wet weather. Slow-growing late-autumn roots risk slug and maggot damage and splitting.
Trim leaves about 1/2 in. above the crown. Store sound roots separately in sand, cool, ventilated and just above freezing; they may keep until March.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Carrot fly	Tunnelled roots.	Use fine mesh; remove thinnings; avoid bruising.
Fanging	Forked roots	Remove stones, improve soil deeply and avoid fresh manure.
Small roots	Small roots; weak growth.	Improve soil; use organic feed if growth is poor.
Splitting	Split roots.	Water evenly; mulch in drought; use split roots now.
Sclerotinia rot	White mould; rotting roots.	Remove diseased roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Carrot-willow aphid	Distorted, stunted leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Black rot	Black lesions on stored roots.	Remove rotten roots; store sound roots; rotate.
Motley dwarf virus	Yellow mottling; red outer leaves.	No cure; remove affected plants. Monitor aphids.
Green top	Green exposed crowns.	Earth up to cover exposed root tops.
Violet root rot	Purple felt-like growth on roots.	Destroy affected roots; never store them; rotate.
Final tips

Avoid fresh manure and disturbance around established roots.

Work from one end of the row when harvesting.

Inspect stored roots and remove any that rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
37

text:
Beetroot.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Beetroot’s sweet, earthy roots suit raw salads, hot dishes, pickles, borsch and chutneys; young leaves are edible too. This cool-climate crop needs well-drained, humus-rich soil and steady moisture. Growth starts slowly, then roots swell quickly. Sow small batches or raise module clumps. Early sowings under cover can give golf-ball-sized roots by late spring; later sowings provide summer, autumn and storage crops. Lift before roots become woody or leathery. In mild winters some can stay outside, but severe frost can freeze and rot them.

Apr – Jun

Harvest

Jun – Nov

Germination

10–14 days

Depth

1 in.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

globe: 10 lb; long: 18 lb

Plant spacing

4 in. between plants

From sowing: globe roots ~11 weeks; long roots ~16 weeks

Recommended varieties
GLOBE · RED
Boltardy

A familiar round red beetroot valued for resistance to bolting. A useful choice for earlier sowings under suitable conditions.

GLOBE · RED
Pablo F1

A round red beetroot producing uniform roots with good kitchen quality. Harvest young for tender roots.

CYLINDRICAL
Cylindra

Long, cylindrical red roots make even slices easy. Useful for cooking and pickling when shape matters more than round presentation.

GLOBE · RED
Chioggia

A heritage beetroot with pink-and-white rings when cut raw. Grow for visual variety alongside a standard red beetroot.

CYLINDRICAL
Forono

An elongated red beetroot with a tidy shape for slicing. Retain as an established alternative to round-rooted selections.

Key risks
Bolting

Plants sometimes run to seed before roots have developed.

Fanging

Forked roots are usually caused by adding fresh manure shortly before sowing.

Mangold fly (leaf miner)

Small white grubs burrow inside the leaves, causing tunnels which later turn into blisters.

Heart rot

Leaves wilt in summer and the tops of the roots develop brown, sunken patches.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
26
ROOT CROPS

A cool-climate crop.

Use well-drained soil rich in organic matter.

Keep moisture steady.

Drought hardens roots; sudden wet can split them.

Sow for a long season.

Successive sowings extend the harvest.

Soil & preparation
Use humus-rich, well-drained soil without fresh manure. Remove stones; long roots need deep, sandy ground.
Use previously manured ground or add autumn compost. Lime acid soil towards pH 6.5; feed poor ground if needed.
Sowing & planting
1 Sow seed clusters

Sow clusters thinly; cover and keep moist.

2 Thin seedlings

Thin direct sowings early to single plants.

Raise early crops in modules; plant clumps intact. Quick facts spacing is for individual, direct-sown plants.

Soak clusters for hours or overnight. Sow warm for early-spring planting; continue into early summer for roots before winter.

Looking after the crop
Thin direct sowings early to single plants; protect from birds. Plant module clumps intact and pick their largest roots first.
Hoe gently; water evenly and moderately. Mulch to hold moisture: drought makes roots woody and reduces yield; sudden wet can split them.
Fleece can bring crops forward, but weed beneath it regularly. Pick young leaves before they toughen and use them like spinach.
Harvesting & storage
Pull globe roots before cricket-ball size. Gently twist larger roots from clumps, letting smaller ones swell; well-kept patches can crop for two months or more.
Fork up storage roots in autumn without piercing them. Discard damaged roots. Twist off foliage, leaving short stalks; do not cut roots.
Roots can stay outside in mild winters, but lift before severe frost. Store sound roots cool in paper sacks or moist sand, without touching.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting	Early flowering; poor roots.	Avoid early sowing; thin promptly; use resistant varieties.
Fanging	Forked roots.	Avoid fresh manure and stones; prepare soil well.
Mangold fly (leaf miner)	Blisters and tunnels in leaves.	Crush larvae in mines; use mesh on a rotated bed.
Heart rot	Brown or black areas inside roots.	Confirm boron shortage; seek organic correction advice.
Blackleg	Seedlings blacken and collapse.	Remove affected seedlings; improve drainage.
Speckled yellows	Yellow patches; rolled edges.	Confirm manganese shortage; avoid excess lime.
Autumnal fungal root rots	Dark rot in wet autumns.	Lift promptly; store only sound roots.
Leaf spot	Brown spots with pale centres.	Remove badly affected leaves; rotate; add compost.
Final tips

Leave four or five seedlings in module clumps.

Take the largest clump roots first, leaving others to swell.

Twist off foliage; do not cut roots for storage.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
27
Growing guide · Beetroot

text:
Leek.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Leeks give sweet white shanks and useful green leaves from late summer through winter and, with suitable varieties, into spring. They gain size as summer crops fade, supplying fresh vegetables in leaner months. Related to onions, they are generally easier and more tolerant, especially in cool, moist conditions. Give them a long season, steady moisture and some blanching; most gardeners raise seedlings to transplant.

Quick facts
Sow

Mar – Apr

Harvest

Oct – Apr

Germination

14–18 days

Depth

5/8 in.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Yield (10 ft row)

10 lb

Plant spacing

Between plants: 6–8 in.; 4 in. for baby leeks

Ready in

From sowing: early crops ~30 weeks; late winter/spring crops ~45 weeks

Growing calendar

Recommended varieties
MID-SEASON
Musselburgh

A traditional hardy leek with thick stems for dependable autumn and winter crops.

MID-SEASON
Oarsman F1

A modern autumn leek with useful rust resistance and healthy foliage.

EARLY
Jolant

An earlier crop for late summer and autumn, complementing hardy winter leeks.

LATE
Below Zero F1

A winter leek for standing through cold weather and extending fresh picking.

Key risks
White rot (mouldy nose)

White rot affects onions, shallots, garlic and leeks.

Allium leaf miner

Adult flies make distinctive rows of small white feeding punctures on allium leaves.

Leek moth

Small creamy-white to pale green caterpillars with brown heads and small legs feed within young leek and onion leaves, producing translucent patches, shredded foliage and sometimes secondary rot.

Rust

Orange pustules appear on allium leaves, especially leeks and garlic.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
62
ONION FAMILY

Keep leeks growing steadily.

Water in dry weather, weed carefully and mulch to hold moisture.

Choose varieties for the season.

Early leeks and hardy winter leeks have different frost tolerance.

Soil & preparation
Use rich, moist, well-drained soil. Add compost or rotted manure to poor ground; avoid compaction.
Previously fed ground is ideal. Test acid soil before liming; keep summer roots moist.
Sowing & planting
1 Lower the leek

Plant May–July: one pencil-thick leek per hole.

2 Water into the hole

Water in rather than filling the hole with dry soil.

Transplant hole Dibbed, 6 in. deep

Sow thinly in a seedbed or modules.

Use fresh seed. Sow outdoors in late March–April; start very early or exhibition crops indoors in late winter.

Clumps: sow 3–4 per module; plant small. Use strong plants; don’t trim healthy roots/leaves.

Looking after the crop
Hoe carefully, water in dry spells and mulch with compost. Let dibbed holes fill naturally after watering-in; do not fill them with dry soil.
Earth up established plants gradually for longer white shanks; keep soil out of leaf joints. Where leek moth is a problem, fit insect mesh as soon as plants go outside.
Harvesting & storage
Lift small leeks first, loosening roots with a fork. Use white shanks and green leaves; the latter suit soups, stews and stocks.
Harvest tender early varieties before severe frost. Hardy winter leeks can stand; lift and heel in a batch before the ground freezes.
Finish spring crops when flower stems appear, before shanks become hard.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
White rot (mouldy nose)	Yellowing; white mould at roots or base.	Remove diseased plants; keep alliums off infected ground.
Allium leaf miner	White puncture rows; internal maggots or pupae.	Mesh during fly activity; remove infested plants and debris.
Leek moth	Leaf mines, shredded leaves; caterpillars inside.	Mesh young crops; remove infested leaves and debris.
Rust	Orange leaf pustules; severe yellowing.	Avoid crowding and excess nitrogen; clear infected debris.
Onion fly	Yellowing or wilting; maggots at roots and stem bases.	Remove affected plants; protect young crops with mesh on a rotated bed.
Bolting	Flower stems form and shanks harden.	Use suitable sowing times; harvest before stems harden.
Stem & bulb eelworm	Swollen, distorted growth; soft bases.	Confirm diagnosis; remove plants and avoid moving affected soil.
White tip	White, papery tips spread down leaves.	Remove badly affected plants; improve drainage and rotate.
Final tips

To clear winter beds, heel leeks into soil/moist sand under cover.

Deeper planting whitens shanks; excess hinders growth/lifting.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
63
Growing guide · Leek
ONION FAMILY

text:
Tomato, Outdoor.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Outdoor tomatoes have plenty of flavour to offer, but need a warm, sunny, sheltered site and a variety suited to British summers. Choose plants labelled for outdoor cultivation; in cooler areas, cloches or other protection can make a crop more reliable. Tall cordon tomatoes need staking, side-shooting and stopping near the end of the season so existing fruit can ripen. Bush or determinate tomatoes need less pruning and can be grown under cloches or in containers. Keep low fruit clear of the ground where practical and check for slugs and blight.

Quick facts
Sow

Mar – Apr

Harvest

Jul – Oct

Germination

8–11 days

Yield per plant

4 lb

Plant spacing

Between plants: 18–24 in., allowing more room for vigorous plants

Ready in

About 20 weeks from sowing

Growing calendar
J
F
M
A
M
J
J
A
S

HARVEST

Bright: usual months · Muted: less usual

Core needs
1 = low · 5 = high
Sun
5/5
Water
4/5

Recommended varieties
CORDON
Outdoor Girl

An early cordon tomato suited to outdoor growing. Provide support and remove sideshoots as for other cordon varieties.

CORDON
Gardener's Delight

A familiar cordon tomato with small red fruits. A useful outdoor choice in a warm, sheltered position.

CORDON
Crimson Crush F1

A cordon tomato bred for outdoor growing with strong late-blight resistance. Produces large red fruits for slicing and cooking.

CORDON
Sungold F1

A sweet orange cherry tomato for a sunny, sheltered outdoor site. Grow as a supported cordon and pick ripe fruits promptly.

BUSH
Red Alert

An early bush tomato with small red fruits. Useful where compact plants are preferred to tall, trained cordons.

Key risks
Blight

Blight causes rapidly spreading brown leaf and stem lesions and fruit decay in damp weather.

Blossom end rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

Slugs

Slugs chew low-hanging fruit, particularly on bush plants.

Split fruit

Ripe fruit may split after irregular watering or rain following dry soil.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
94
FRUITING CROPS

Choose a suitable outdoor variety.

Early cropping and a warm, sheltered site improve the chance of ripe fruit.

Keep watering even.

Dry-to-wet swings split fruit and can encourage blossom-end rot.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained soil with mature compost in a sunny, sheltered spot. Improve heavy clay well before planting.
Pots/growbags suit patios or small spaces; water frequently and feed organically regularly.
Sowing & planting
1 Grow on and harden

Raise seedlings under cover in spring or buy sturdy pot-grown plants. Harden off gradually before planting outside.

2 Plant beside support

After frost risk, plant in settled warmth. Water first; keep the rootball intact and set slightly deeper. Support tall types; tie in regularly.

Bush/basket types: use packet spacing; support heavy stems. No routine side-shooting.

Sow under cover in March–early April; plant outside in settled, warm late-spring weather after frost risk.

Looking after the crop
Support cordons; tie about every 12 in. and remove side shoots around 1 in. long. Stop above the last useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; keep healthy foliage. Bushes normally need no side-shooting or stopping.
Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Ventilate cloches in warmth: they reduce rain on leaves; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; keep stalks where possible, avoid skin damage and use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October; bushes July–September. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors at season’s end. Ripen in shallow trays at room temperature; check for rot. A ripe apple or banana nearby helps. Use tested bottling or green-tomato chutney recipes.
Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
Blight — Brown dying leaves; dark fruit rot.	Remove infected plants; keep foliage dry where practical.
Blossom end rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
Slugs — Low fruit is chewed or hollowed.	Keep fruit off soil; check and hand-pick near vulnerable plants.
Split fruit — Fruit cracks after rain or uneven watering.	Keep root moisture steady and mulch.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Blossom drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Cutworms — Young stems are severed near soil level.	Protect seedlings with collars; inspect nearby soil.
Final tips

Check beneath bush foliage often: ripe fruit and slug damage are easily missed.

Stop tall plants in time for the local season; leave two leaves above the final truss.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
95
Growing guide · Tomato, Outdoor

  1. Use fertile, well-drained soil with mature compost in a sunny, sheltered spot. Improve heavy clay well before planting.
  2. Pots/growbags suit patios or small spaces; water frequently and feed organically regularly.

Sowing & planting

1 Grow on and harden

Raise seedlings under cover in spring or buy sturdy pot-grown plants. Harden off gradually before planting outside.

2 Plant beside support

After frost risk, plant in settled warmth. Water first; keep the rootball intact and set slightly deeper. Support tall types; tie in regularly.

Bush/basket types: use packet spacing; support heavy stems. No routine side-shooting.

Sow under cover in March–early April; plant outside in settled, warm late-spring weather after frost risk.

Looking after the crop

  1. Support cordons; tie about every 12 in. and remove side shoots around 1 in. long. Stop above the last useful truss by late summer. Remove yellow leaves sparingly; keep healthy foliage. Bushes normally need no side-shooting or stopping.
  2. Water roots steadily; feed organically as fruit develops. Keep low fruit off wet soil. Ventilate cloches in warmth: they reduce rain on leaves; fleece does not prevent blight. Check for blight.

Harvesting & storage

  1. Pick fully coloured fruit gently; keep stalks where possible, avoid skin damage and use promptly. Tall types often crop August–October; bushes July–September. Bring sound unripe fruit indoors at season’s end. Ripen in shallow trays at room temperature; check for rot. A ripe apple or banana nearby helps. Use tested bottling or green-tomato chutney recipes.

Pests & diseases

Problem · what to look forWhat to do
Blight — Brown dying leaves; dark fruit rot.Remove infected plants; keep foliage dry where practical.
Blossom end rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
Slugs — Low fruit is chewed or hollowed.Keep fruit off soil; check and hand-pick near vulnerable plants.
Split fruit — Fruit cracks after rain or uneven watering.Keep root moisture steady and mulch.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.Tolerate light colonies; squash damaging ones; encourage predators.
Grey mould (Botrytis) — Grey mould on damaged stems or fruit.Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Virus — Leaves mottled and distorted; plants stunted.Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Blossom drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Cutworms — Young stems are severed near soil level.Protect seedlings with collars; inspect nearby soil.

Final tips

Check beneath bush foliage often: ripe fruit and slug damage are easily missed.

Stop tall plants in time for the local season; leave two leaves above the final truss.

Potatoes give heavy crops from small plots; check old grassland for wireworms. Plant seed tubers, not true seed, and keep new tubers covered: light makes them green and poisonous. Eat first/second earlies fresh. Maincrops yield and store better, but need more space and face more blight. Give rich soil and moisture; guard frost-tender leaves. Lift gently; store maincrops cool, dark and frost-free.

Key risks
Blight

Potato blight spreads rapidly in warm, wet weather, causing brown foliage lesions, collapse and potentially tuber decay.

Slugs

Slugs tunnel into tubers, particularly in damp soil or beneath covers and mulches.

Scab

Common scab causes corky skin patches and is favoured by dry conditions as tubers form, particularly in alkaline soil.

Eelworm

Potato cyst nematodes can build up where potatoes are grown repeatedly.

ROOT CROPS

Keep developing tubers covered.

Earth or mulch excludes light; do not eat green potatoes.

Choose the crop for your needs.

Earlies give fresh new potatoes; maincrops give larger storage harvests.

Soil & preparation
Fertile, slightly acid soil with rotted compost/manure. Rotate; avoid liming.
Check new ground for slugs/wireworms. Avoid frost pockets and waterlogging.
Sowing & planting
1 Sprouts upwards

Set seed tubers at trench base, sprouts up.

2 Cover gently

Cover gently; protect sprouts. Water well.

First-early rows 24 in. between rows
Maincrop rows 30 in. between rows

Or use holes. No-dig: shallow-plant under thick, light-excluding mulch. Chitting benefits earlies most.

Plant earlies March–April, maincrops April, conditions permitting. Drain pots; give ample compost.

Looking after the crop
Protect shoots from frost. Earth up or mulch before tubers are exposed; weed carefully and water as tubers swell, especially in pots.
If blight becomes established, remove affected haulm and debris. Where conditions permit, wait about two weeks before lifting; use sound tubers promptly.
Harvesting & storage
Test-lift earlies at a useful size; flowering alone is unreliable. Use fresh. Fork storage crops after haulm dies, before severe frost. Collect every tuber, including tiny ones, to reduce volunteers and disease carry-over.
Dry briefly out of strong light. Store sound, dry tubers cool, dark and frost-free in breathable jute, canvas or paper sacks, never sealed plastic. Use sound damaged tubers first; discard rot.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Blight	Brown collapsing foliage; tubers may rot.	Remove affected haulm; allow skins to set before lifting where possible.
Slugs	Deep tunnels spoil tubers.	Avoid slug refuges; lift mature crops promptly.
Scab	Corky skin patches on tubers.	Avoid liming; keep soil moist as tubers form.
Eelworm	Stunted patches; cysts on roots.	Rotate; use suitable resistant varieties after diagnosis.
Frost	Young foliage blackens.	Cover shoots before frost; unfrozen plants may regrow.
Storage rots	Tubers soften or decay in store.	Store only sound dry tubers; inspect and remove rot.
Blackleg	Stem bases blacken; leaves wilt.	Remove affected plants; use healthy certified seed.
Wireworm	Narrow tunnels riddle tubers.	Avoid infested ground; remove larvae and lift promptly.
Wart disease	Cauliflower-like growths around eyes.	Do not move soil or tubers; report for official diagnosis.
Colorado beetle	Striped yellow beetles or spotted larvae.	Contain securely, photograph and report; do not release.
Final tips

Check mulch/ridges often. Keep tubers covered; never eat green ones.

Check stores often; remove soft or rotten tubers to stop decay.
